transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Atlas Lead ML Eng), Mei (Platform Eng), Ravi (CTO)
Artifacts referenced: Atlas batch traces (link: customer:/atlas/traces_48h.csv), Redwood slot-sizing deck (link: https://redwood.app/notes/slot-sizing), sample bench repo (https://github.com/redwood/bench-sched)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, welcome, thanks for carving time today, this is the throughput sync, real quick on agenda, priya will walk scheduler knobs and k/v prefetch ideas, then we can go into your traces and plan a bench run.

[00:18] Carlos: thanks, yeah we got a couple of pain points — spikes during batch ingestion, tail latency jumps, and our kv hit-rate is kinda low on cold starts.

[00:32] Priya: cool, that's what we'll focus on. high level: continuous batching helps, but the scheduler params — slot_size, max_num_seqs, and window_ms — are where you tune latency vs throughput. also kv prefetch/prewarm is big for your cold path.

[00:48] Mei: quick question, on-prem constraints: we have limited GPUs per rack and slower interconnects compared to cloud. does that change slot sizing?

[00:56] Priya: yes, absolutely. slot_size is effectively how many concurrent seqs we group for kernel execution. on slower interconnect or smaller mem GPUs, you want smaller slot_size to avoid cross-device stalls. but that reduces batching efficiency. so it's a tradeoff.

[01:20] Ravi: when you say smaller, like 8 versus 32? what's the ballpark?

[01:28] Priya: in our experience, for consumer grade 40GB GPUs with on-prem networking, slot_size of 8-16 tends to keep tail latency reasonable. in hosted high-throughput infra you push 32-64. but it depends on model seq-len distribution.

[01:45] Carlos: we run a mix: many short prompts (avg 40 tokens) and some longer synth steps up to 1,500 tokens. how do we pick max_num_seqs?

[01:54] Priya: max_num_seqs is the scheduler cap on how many sequences can be active in a slot iteration. if you set it too small, long sequences block throughput for short ones; set too large and you blow memory and increase latency for cold kv misses. we suggest profiling with two knobs: 32 and 64, and measure tail p99 for short prompts and throughput for long jobs.

[02:18] Jordan: real quick note — we saw in your traces a long tail around 800ms during peak. likely caused by KV cache miss + large attention workspace allocation.

[02:27] Carlos: yes, that's what we thought. our kv hit-rate hovers 65% on average, but drops dramatically during bursts. any recommended prefetch strategies?

[02:38] Priya: two patterns that work: 1) predictive prefetch where we keep prefix KV for active sessions in a small warm pool, and 2) staggered prewarm during autoscaler scale-up: as a new slot becomes hot we proactively load common prefixes. predictive prefetch needs a bit of telemetry — LRU isn't enough, you want frequency+recency.

[03:02] Mei: telemetry is doable, we can export top-50 prefixes and session ids. is there risk to memory pressure with prefetch?

[03:08] Priya: yes — that's why we bound prefetch size per slot and evict by estimated token cost. set a prefetch_budget_per_slot (we call it prefetch_tokens) — e.g., 20k tokens per slot; tune based on mem.

[03:24] [00:03:24] Carlos: ok, makes sense. what about token ceilings? we have a p99 latency target of 450ms for short prompts — do we enforce token limits server-side?

[03:34] Priya: enforce soft token ceilings at the router for non-critical paths — this prevents long generations from monopolizing slots. also use adaptive token ceilings: higher during low load, lower during peaks. the scheduler can apply token_limit per-request override.

[03:50] Ravi: curious — how does quantization affect these numbers? we tested int8 on some models and saw lower throughput in some cases.

[03:59] Priya: quantization cuts memory but may increase compute time for some kernels if not supported by optimized paths. for decoder stacks, int8 often reduces bandwidth pressure and helps throughput; but on certain older kernels we saw 5-10% extra per-token latency. we generally recommend mixed strategy: use int8 where latency improves in bench and keep fp16 for tail-critical routes.

[04:19] Jordan: we built a small decision rule: if p50 < 60ms and p99 < 400ms on int8 bench then default to int8; otherwise leave fp16 for that model.

[04:28] [00:04:28] Carlos: can we walk through a concrete bench config? like which metrics you want from our traces?

[04:35] Priya: sure. send: per-request seq_len, prompt distribution, arrival timestamp, tenant_id. we'll synthesize arrival patterns and run bench with these knobs toggled: slot_size {8,16,32}, max_num_seqs {16,32,64}, window_ms {5,10,20}, prefetch_tokens {0,10000,20000}, token_limit {512,1024,2048}. we'll capture p50/p90/p99 latency, GPU utilization, and KV hit-rate.

[05:05] Mei: we've got those traces, we'll scrub PII and upload. what's a realistic expected delta if we enable prefetch and push slot_size from 8 to 16?

[05:13] Priya: ballpark: throughput up 10-25% with small tail-latency risk. biggest wins come from reducing cold-kv misses — prefetch can reduce p99 by 30-50% during scale-up if you target the right prefixes.

[05:28] Ravi: interesting. what about autoscaler slot sizing? our current autoscaler grows by GPU count, not by slot_count. is that correct?

[05:36] Jordan: yes, most infra scales GPUs. but Redwood's autoscaler can scale slots independently — each GPU can host N slots. this matters because when you scale, you want to avoid many cold slots coming up at once. we recommend staged warmup: bring slots up in waves so prewarming can catch up.

[05:54] Priya: exactly — if you spin up 8 new slots simultaneously, kv miss storms happen. staged growth (2-3 slots at a time with a small delay) plus prefetch reduces the miss spike. also set a slot_startup_delay_ms to allow background prewarm.

[06:10] [00:06:10] Carlos: for on-prem, our startup memory is a concern. how much prewarm overhead per slot should we expect?

[06:18] Priya: depends on prefix size; for typical conversational prefixes, assume ~200-400KB per prefix in the KV structure; preloading 50 prefixes ~20MB; with 8 slots that's 160MB — still small relative to 40GB GPU but multiply by many tenants and it adds. so cap prefetch.

[06:38] Mei: does Redwood provide tooling to estimate that automatically?

[06:42] Priya: yes — our slot-sizing script ingests sample traces and outputs estimated mem per-slot under given prefetch_budget and avg prefix size. we'll share that script in the deck. (link shared in chat)

[06:55] Ravi: any gotchas with multi-tenant fairness? we want to avoid noisy-tenant causing other tenants' latency to spike.

[07:03] Priya: use priority windows and per-tenant token quotas. scheduler supports tenant-aware batching where we attempt fair share by limiting number of concurrent seqs per tenant inside a slot (tenant_max_seqs). this reduces noisy neighbor effects.

[07:18] Jordan: we can also enable request-level admission control: low-priority background jobs get preempted by interactive user requests.

[07:26] Carlos: let's talk about fallback strategies. during overload do you prefer degrading model size, or increasing batching and risking latency?

[07:33] Priya: fallback lattice: 1) shed non-critical traffic, 2) fallback to smaller quantized model variant (if quality acceptable), 3) increase batching aggressively but only for background queues. for interactive paths we avoid batching that harms p99.

[07:48] [00:07:48] Mei: we saw mentions of 'kv prefetch by prefix popularity' — how do you compute popularity?

[07:54] Priya: we use a frequency-over-window metric: count(prefix_hits) / window_seconds weighted by recency. it's simple and avoids complex ML. maintain a top-K hot-prefix list per region.

[08:08] Carlos: is there risk of prefetching sensitive data? some prefixes contain PHI for us.

[08:15] Priya: good call. prefetch only index tokens, never payloads, and for PHI prefixes you can disable prefetch or encrypt with customer KMS. Redwood supports KMS integration for on-prem and private deployments. we'll include security doc.

[08:32] Jordan: sharing the security checklist after the call.

[08:36] [00:08:36] Carlos: switching gears — we noticed scheduler queue stalls when many long generations are in-flight. what's the best mitigation?

[08:44] Priya: two common mitigations: 1) per-request token_limit and 2) dynamic max_num_seqs throttling — temporarily reduce max_num_seqs when the long-gen ratio exceeds threshold. we also recommend early-termination heuristics for background tasks.

[09:02] Mei: can the router signal the scheduler to lower max_num_seqs dynamically?

[09:08] Priya: yes, via the control plane we push a policy update; we also support an automatic heuristic that observes backlog and reduces window_ms and max_num_seqs. we'll demo this in the bench.

[09:18] Carlos: for the bench, should we simulate long tails, or replay real traces?

[09:23] Priya: do both. replay traces to validate existing behavior, then run synthetic bursts to stress fallback. synthetic tests help expose scheduling edge-cases.

[09:34] [00:09:34] Jordan: a question from sales-side — cost impact. if we prewarm and increase slot_size, do we see higher infra cost?

[09:41] Priya: prewarm costs are mostly memory and small compute to load kv, the main cost change is improved throughput which usually reduces per-token GPU time, lowering unit cost. but if you over-provision slots and keep them idle, cost rises. that's why autoscaler policy matters.

[09:58] Ravi: curious about real numbers: any prior POC numbers you can share?

[10:03] Priya: in a customer POC with mixed short/long workload, we cut p99 by ~40% and improved overall throughput by 18% after tuning slot_size from 89 to 16 and enabling targeted prefetch. we'll redact names and share the summary.

[10:18] Carlos: that sounds promising. what about KV eviction policies? we currently use strict LRU.

[10:25] Priya: LRU is ok but for prefix caching popularity decay means you want frequency+recency and a small probationary window. also consider size-aware eviction: evict large prefixes first if memory pressures spike.

[10:40] Mei: are there observability hooks we can add? we want per-slot k/v hit-rate, prefetch queue size, and slot startup times in the dashboard.

[10:49] Priya: yes — Redwood Console has token-level breakdown per-route and per-slot KPIs. we'll provide a dashboard template: KV hit-rate, prefetch_budget_used, slot_startup_latency, GPU_util, p50/p99 per-tenant.

[11:05] [00:11:05] Jordan: let's talk about kernel selection effects: some models have kerning ops that don't scale linearly with batch size. any easy signals?

[11:13] Priya: look at per-kernel timing breakdown. if attention kernels dominate and don't shrink with larger batch, increasing slot_size may hurt. our runtime switches kernels based on seq_len distribution and will pick fused attention when beneficial. the bench will surface that.

[11:30] Carlos: how long do these bench runs take? we have a small test cluster for POCs.

[11:36] Priya: a replay run for 48h traces on a modest cluster usually takes 2-4 hours depending on acceleration; synthetic stress tests are faster. plan for ~1 day to iterate configs.

[11:46] Mei: on the practical side, we need a checklist for on-prem install to avoid cold storms during initial rollout.

[11:53] Priya: we'll send an on-prem playbook: staggered rollout with prewarm windows, initial conservative slot_size, monitored kv hit-rate gating, and a canary traffic split. include rollback steps.

[12:05] [00:12:05] Carlos: great. earlier you mentioned tenant_max_seqs — any defaults?

[12:11] Priya: default tenant_max_seqs = 8 for interactive tenants on shared clusters; increase for trusted tenants on Dedicated. tune based on tenant footprint.

[12:21] Ravi: ok, final high-level ask from us: we need to see a bench with our traces and a proposed slot-sizing plan for our on-prem racks by next week. feasible?

[12:30] Jordan: yes — Priya will run bench and we'll share slot-sizing deck + security doc.

[12:35] Priya: I'll need the scrubbed traces and a short note on your desired SLOs. we will run the matrix I mentioned.

[12:43] Carlos: we'll upload traces by EOD tomorrow. one more question — during scale-down, do slots flush kv? what's the impact?

[12:50] Priya: on scale-down we try to keep one hot slot per GPU to retain hot prefixes. if you aggressively remove slots, you lose KV and see misses. configure graceful_scale_down and graceful_shutdown_delay to give prewarm time to migrate or to keep hot slots.

[13:05] Mei: good to know. any tips for reducing network burst when prefetching during startup?

[13:12] Priya: stagger prefetch with jitter and rate-limit prefetch bandwidth per-slot. also employ region-local prefix caches so you don't cross AZs for prefetch.

[13:26] [00:13:26] Jordan: wrapping up, do we have any open blockers?

[13:30] Carlos: none besides getting the traces to you and confirming the POC cluster specs.

[13:36] Priya: perfect. I'll start with two bench runs: replay then synthetic burst. will post results and a recommended slot config.

[13:44] Jordan: I'll send pricing and the VPC/on-prem checklist. also a short note on KMS options.

[13:50] Ravi: thanks everyone, this was useful. looking forward to the bench.

[13:54] Mei: thanks, see ya.

[14:00] End of recording.

Notes: occasional transcription errors: 'slot_size' transcribed as 'slot-size' in a couple places, 'kv' as 'k/v' or 'K V', and a few timestamps drifted due to generator. Action items captured in metadata.
